title: Which Modern Literature Text Is Best?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles reverse-engineers GCSE English Literature text selection from the examiner's chair rather than the reader's, using a staged conversation with Gemini to model the reasoning. His central move is to treat AQA's Level descriptors as a design brief: since Level 6 rewards students who argue that characters are 'constructs' delivering an authorial message rather than real people, the texts that pay off best are those with blatant, polemical, structurally rigid messaging. On this logic he ranks An Inspector Calls as the safest Level 6 vehicle for drama but flags Leave Taking as his personal pick for a school willing to trade familiarity for freshness, since examiners fatigued by thousands of identical Inspector Calls essays reward novelty. For prose he favours Lord of the Flies over Animal Farm because its symbolic density supports AO2 language analysis, whereas Animal Farm tempts students into writing a history essay about the Russian Revolution instead of analysing method. Salles extends the same framework to a high-ability Grades 7-9 cohort, arguing that texts richest in ambiguity and construction (DNA, Leave Taking, Pigeon English) let top students argue about how a text is built rather than simply what happens in it. Throughout, the piece is candid that this is a strategic calculus about mark-scheme optimisation, not a claim about literary merit, and closes by inviting departments to weigh text choice against cultural breadth and their EAL cohort makeup.
points: Salles reframes GCSE text choice as reverse-engineering the AQA Level 6 descriptor ('convincing and conceptualised'), arguing the winning texts are ones whose characters read as constructs delivering a polemical message rather than real people.

He warns that popularity is a hidden cost: because over 80% of cohorts study An Inspector Calls, examiner fatigue makes it harder to stand out at the top grades, which is his practical case for switching to Leave Taking.

Golding's Lord of the Flies is preferred over Orwell's Animal Farm specifically because its symbolic density forces AO2 language analysis, while Animal Farm's obvious allegory tempts students into writing a history essay instead.

For Grades 7-9 cohorts, Salles argues the highest-ceiling texts are those rich in ambiguity and structural complexity (DNA, Leave Taking, Pigeon English) because they let students argue about how the text is constructed, not just what it depicts.

He documents a real case of a school switching from An Inspector Calls to Animal Farm two months before the exam and seeing results improve, offered as evidence that text-choice decisions can be made and reversed late in the cycle.
quotes: To get Level 6, a student must argue that the characters are not real people, but vehicles for the author's ideas. Therefore, the texts that lead to the highest grades are those where the author's message is blatant, polemical, and structurally rigid.

My analysis in many schools reveals that the more common the text, the harder it is to get top grades - examiners simply know the text too well. Over 80% of students study An Inspector Calls, so even the great answers read like same old same old.
Last year, I helped a school switch in March of year 11. That's right, 2 months before the exam. They ditched An Inspector Calls and taught Animal Farm, and results went up.
Golding's rich prose forces students to analyse language; Orwell's plain style can leave them with nothing to say about 'methods.'
To hit Level 6 ('Convincing, Critical, Conceptualized'), students need texts that allow them to argue about the construction of the text, not just the characters.
Excluded: Animal Farm. Grade 9 students are often tempted to show off their historical knowledge (Russian Revolution) at the expense of language analysis. It is a 'trap' text for bright students.
Also, Blood Brothers is one of the worst plays I've ever seen - it is always a standing ovation, but I kept my seat warm.
